claim: Huntington's disease is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in Huntingtin (HTT).
source: Caused by a CAG repeat expansion in Huntingtin (HTT) (The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993), HD pathology is prominent in the striatum and cortex, yet transcriptomic studies consistently reveal thousands of changes in gene expression across the brain and different neuronal cell types, involving pathways ranging from autophagy to vesicular trafficking (Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993, which is a reference to published research.

claim: HD pathology is prominent in the striatum and cortex.
source: Caused by a CAG repeat expansion in Huntingtin (HTT) (The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993), HD pathology is prominent in the striatum and cortex, yet transcriptomic studies consistently reveal thousands of changes in gene expression across the brain and different neuronal cell types, involving pathways ranging from autophagy to vesicular trafficking (Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about HD pathology and is cited in the context of transcriptomic studies.

claim: Transcriptomic studies in HD reveal thousands of changes in gene expression across the brain and different neuronal cell types.
source: Caused by a CAG repeat expansion in Huntingtin (HTT) (The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993), HD pathology is prominent in the striatum and cortex, yet transcriptomic studies consistently reveal thousands of changes in gene expression across the brain and different neuronal cell types, involving pathways ranging from autophagy to vesicular trafficking (Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saudou and Humbert, 2016, which reviews transcriptomic findings in HD.

claim: HD pathogenesis is driven by upregulation of genes involved in the actin cytoskeleton and inflammation.
source: This study demonstrated that HD pathogenesis is driven by upregulation of genes involved in the actin cytoskeleton and inflammation, but that neurons compensate by downregulating the expression of genes involved in synaptic biology and calcium signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a previous study by the authors (Al-Ramahi et al., 2018), which integrated transcriptomics with in vivo screening.

claim: Neurons compensate for HD pathogenesis by downregulating the expression of genes involved in synaptic biology and calcium signaling.
source: This study demonstrated that HD pathogenesis is driven by upregulation of genes involved in the actin cytoskeleton and inflammation, but that neurons compensate by downregulating the expression of genes involved in synaptic biology and calcium signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from a previous study by the authors (Al-Ramahi et al., 2018).

claim: HTT is necessary for normal synaptogenesis and maintenance within the cortico-striatal circuit.
source: The finding that synaptic changes were protective caught our attention because HTT itself is necessary for normal synaptogenesis and maintenance within the cortico-striatal circuit (McKinstry et al., 2014), largely through its role in retrograde axonal trafficking of neurotrophic factors (Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McKinstry et al., 2014.

claim: HTT plays a role in retrograde axonal trafficking of neurotrophic factors.
source: The finding that synaptic changes were protective caught our attention because HTT itself is necessary for normal synaptogenesis and maintenance within the cortico-striatal circuit (McKinstry et al., 2014), largely through its role in retrograde axonal trafficking of neurotrophic factors (Saudou and Humbert, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saudou and Humbert, 2016.

claim: Glial cells contribute to synapse formation, function, and elimination.
source: But synapses involve more than just neurons: glial cells also contribute to synapse formation, function, and elimination (Filipello et al., 2018; McKinstry et al., 2014; Octeau et al., 2018; Stogsdill et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Filipello et al., 2018; McKinstry et al., 2014; Octeau et al., 2018; Stogsdill et al., 2017).

claim: The accumulation of mutant Huntingtin (mHTT) in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes hinders their development and function and contributes to disease pathophysiology.
source: The accumulation of mutant Huntingtin(mHTT) in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes hinders their development and function and contributes to disease pathophysiology (Benraiss et al., 2016; Ferrari Bardile et al., 2019; Osipovitch et al., 2019; Wood et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Benraiss et al., 2016; Ferrari Bardile et al., 2019; Osipovitch et al., 2019; Wood et al., 2018).

claim: Healthy glia can improve the disease phenotype in HD mice.
source: Conversely, healthy glia can improve the disease phenotype in HD mice (Benraiss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Benraiss et al., 2016.

claim: 1852 genes were downregulated in HD patient striata compared to healthy individuals.
source: We identified 1852 downregulated and 1941 upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in patients with HD compared to healthy individuals (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis of human post-mortem striatal samples presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 1941 genes were upregulated in HD patient striata compared to healthy individuals.
source: We identified 1852 downregulated and 1941 upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in patients with HD compared to healthy individuals (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on data analysis of human post-mortem striatal samples presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 3575 genes were downregulated in HD mouse striata compared to wildtype mice.
source: Comparing the striata of wildtype mice to the knock-in HD mouse models, there were 3575 downregulated and 3634 upregulated DEGs (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on reanalysis of published RNA-seq data from HD knock-in mouse models presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 3634 genes were upregulated in HD mouse striata compared to wildtype mice.
source: Comparing the striata of wildtype mice to the knock-in HD mouse models, there were 3575 downregulated and 3634 upregulated DEGs (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on reanalysis of published RNA-seq data from HD knock-in mouse models presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Expressing mHTT in neurons resulted in 3058 downregulated and 2979 upregulated DEGs in Drosophila.
source: Expressing mHTT in neurons resulted in 3058 downregulated and 2979 upregulated DEGs, while expressing mHTT in glia resulted in 3127 downregulated and 3159 upregulated DEGs.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data from Drosophila HD models generated in this study.

claim: Expressing mHTT in glia resulted in 3127 downregulated and 3159 upregulated DEGs in Drosophila.
source: Expressing mHTT in neurons resulted in 3058 downregulated and 2979 upregulated DEGs, while expressing mHTT in glia resulted in 3127 downregulated and 3159 upregulated DEGs.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data from Drosophila HD models generated in this study.

claim: 1293 genes were downregulated and 1181 genes were upregulated in both neurons and glia expressing mHTT in Drosophila.
source: There were also DEGs common to both neurons and glia expressing mHTT: 1293 downregulated and 1181 upregulated (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA-seq data from Drosophila HD models presented in Figure 1B.

claim: 815 upregulated DEGs observed in HD patient-derived striatal tissue had an orthologous gene in the HD mouse model and at least one Drosophila model of HD that was concordantly upregulated.
source: 815 upregulated DEGs observed in HD patient-derived striatal tissue had an orthologous gene in the HD mouse model and at least one Drosophila model of HD that was concordantly upregulated.
evidence: The claim is based on comparative transcriptomic analysis across three species using a graph-based approach.

claim: 791 DEGs identified in HD patients had an orthologous gene in mouse and Drosophila models that was concordantly downregulated.
source: Similarly, 791 DEGs identified in HD patients had an orthologous gene in mouse and Drosophila models that was concordantly downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative transcriptomic analysis across three species presented in Figure 1C.

claim: About 40% of the alterations in gene expression in patient striatal samples are concordant with orthologous genes in both Drosophila and mice models of HD.
source: About 40% of the alterations in gene expression in patient striatal samples are concordant with orthologous genes in both Drosophila and mice models of HD.
evidence: The claim is based on the proportion of concordant DEGs identified in the comparative analysis.

claim: The overlap of concordant, orthologous DEGs across the various HD models was not random (p=6.37×10−158 and p=1.66×10−165).
source: Based on the resulting distribution, we concluded that the overlap of concordant, orthologous DEGs across the various HD models was not random (p=6.37×10−158 and p=1.66×10−165, probability distribution test).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis using a probability distribution test with 20,000 random samplings.

claim: 83.7% of upregulated DEGs and 77.7% of downregulated DEGs that were altered concordantly in human and mouse HD striata were also concordantly altered in the brains of the neuronal and/or glial HD Drosophila models.
source: We found that 83.7% of upregulated DEGs and 77.7% of downregulated DEGs that were altered concordantly in human and mouse HD striata were also concordantly altered in the brains of the neuronal and/or glial HD Drosophila models (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on comparative analysis of concordant DEGs presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The upregulated and downregulated networks of DEGs responding to mHTT expression in neurons or glia had a significant PPI enrichment compared to networks constructed from an equivalent number of random genes selected from a whole-proteome background.
source: The upregulated and downregulated networks of DEGs responding to mHTT expression in neurons or glia had a significant PPI enrichment compared to networks constructed from an equivalent number of random genes selected from a whole-proteome background (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING-db database.

claim: The glial and neuronal networks show higher network connectivity than expected by random chance among proteins present in the striatum.
source: Using average node degree and betweenness as proxies for connectivity, we found that the glial and neuronal networks show higher network connectivity than expected by random chance among proteins present in the striatum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on network analysis comparing connectivity metrics to random striatal protein networks.

claim: The glial networks formed 23 and 24 clusters for upregulated and downregulated DEGs, respectively.
source: The glial networks formed 23 and 24 clusters for upregulated and downregulated DEGs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on clustering analysis using the InfoMap random walks algorithm.

claim: Both the upregulated and downregulated neuronal networks formed 29 clusters.
source: Both the upregulated and downregulated neuronal networks formed 29 clusters.
evidence: The claim is based on clustering analysis using the InfoMap random walks algorithm.

claim: Both the glial and neuronal networks formed significantly more clusters than would be expected from random selection.
source: Both the glial and neuronal networks formed significantly more clusters than would be expected from random selection (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison to networks of randomly selected striatal proteins.

claim: There were 14 clusters of upregulated DEGs common to both glial and neuronal networks.
source: We compared the membership within clusters across the glial and neuronal networks using a pairwise hypergeometric test and identified 14 clusters of upregulated DEGs common to both glial and neuronal networks.
evidence: The claim is based on pairwise hypergeometric test comparing cluster membership.

claim: There were 15 clusters of downregulated DEGs common to both glial and neuronal networks.
source: Similarly, there were 15 clusters of downregulated DEGs common to the both networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on pairwise hypergeometric test comparing cluster membership, presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Six clusters were specifically upregulated in response to mHTT expression in glia, enriched in genes involved in transcription and chromatin remodeling, amino acid metabolism, cell proliferation, cytokine signaling/innate immunity, arachidonic acid metabolism, and steroid synthesis.
source: Six clusters were specifically upregulated in response to mHTT expression, enriched in genes involved in transcription and chromatin remodeling, amino acid metabolism, cell proliferation, cytokine signaling/innate immunity, arachidonic acid metabolism, and steroid synthesis (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of glial-specific clusters presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Six clusters were downregulated in response to glial mHTT expression, containing genes involved in synapse assembly, calcium ion transport, immune system regulation, phagocytosis, mRNA processing, and fatty acid degradation.
source: Six clusters were downregulated in response to glial mHTT expression, containing genes involved in synapse assembly, calcium ion transport, immune system regulation, phagocytosis, mRNA processing, and fatty acid degradation (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of glial-specific clusters presented in Figure 2B.

claim: 46 upregulated and 91 downregulated DEGs were common between conserved HD DEGs from flies expressing mHTT in glia and HD OPCs.
source: We identified 46 upregulated and 91 downregulated DEGs in common (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of DEGs from Drosophila glial mHTT expression and human HD OPCs, presented in Figure 3A.

claim: APCs had 4 upregulated and 12 downregulated genes in common with conserved HD DEGs from flies expressing mHTT in glia.
source: APCs had 4 upregulated and 12 downregulated genes in common.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of DEGs from Drosophila glial mHTT expression and human HD APCs.

claim: The Synapse Assembly cluster was significantly enriched in genes with reduced expression in HD OPCs (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001).
source: We next asked whether any clusters in the fly glial networks were enriched in genes dysregulated in HD OPCs or APCs. The Synapse Assembly cluster (Figure 2B) was significantly enriched in genes with reduced expression in HD OPCs (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001), including SYT13, LRRTM1, GRM1, EPB41L2, DLGAP3, and AGAP2; the only gene of this cluster that was upregulated in HD OPCs was NRXN3 (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is based on Fisher's exact test comparing gene membership between the Synapse Assembly cluster and HD OPC DEGs.

claim: NRXN3 was the only gene in the Synapse Assembly cluster that was upregulated in HD OPCs.
source: The Synapse Assembly cluster (Figure 2B) was significantly enriched in genes with reduced expression in HD OPCs (Fisher's exact test, p<0.001), including SYT13, LRRTM1, GRM1, EPB41L2, DLGAP3, and AGAP2; the only gene of this cluster that was upregulated in HD OPCs was NRXN3 (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of gene expression in HD OPCs, presented in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Diminishing expression of the Drosophila orthologs of SYT13, LRRTM1, GRM1, EPB41L2, DLGAP3, and AGAP2 mitigated the behavioral deficits induced by mHTT expression in glia.
source: We performed genetic perturbation analysis on the Drosophila orthologs of these genes to assess whether their downregulation was pathogenic or compensatory in glia. Diminishing expression of the Drosophila orthologs of these six genes mitigated the behavioral deficits induced by mHTT expression in glia (Figure 3D, additional controls in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data from Drosophila expressing mHTT in glia with reduced expression of these genes, presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Reduced expression of SYT13, LRRTM1, GRM1, EPB41L2, DLGAP3, and AGAP2 is a compensatory response to mHTT expression in glia.
source: We concluded that reduced expression of these genes is a compensatory response to mHTT expression in glia.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral assay results showing that further reducing expression of these genes is protective.

claim: Reducing expression of NLGN3, NLGN4X, HOMER1, and SLITRK5 was protective against glial mHTT toxicity.
source: In our behavioral assay, reducing expression of these interactors, including NLGN3, NLGN4X, HOMER1, and SLITRK5, was also protective against glial mHTT toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4; additional controls in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NRXN3 expression was lower in the bulk HD transcriptome across species compared to their respective controls.
source: NRXN3 expression was lower in the bulk HD transcriptome across species compared to their respective controls, but it was more highly expressed in the HD OPCs than in controls.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of NRXN3 expression in bulk tissue transcriptomes versus single-cell-type profiles.

claim: NRXN3 was more highly expressed in the HD OPCs than in controls.
source: NRXN3 expression was lower in the bulk HD transcriptome across species compared to their respective controls, but it was more highly expressed in the HD OPCs than in controls.
evidence: The claim is based on gene expression data from HD OPCs.

claim: Heterozygous loss of dNRXN3 function in animals expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia mitigated mHTT toxicity and improved behavior.
source: In the Drosophila behavioral assay, heterozygous loss of dNRXN3 function in animals expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia mitigated mHTT toxicity and improved behavior (Figure 4A, left panel).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Heterozygous loss of dNRXN3 function in animals expressing mHTT only in glia mitigated mHTT toxicity and improved behavior.
source: Reproducing this experiment with flies expressing mHTT only in glia yielded the same benefit (Figure 4A, middle panel).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Heterozygous loss of dNRXN3 function did not protect against mHTT pathogenesis in neurons.
source: The obvious next question, given its canonical role in neuron-neuron contact, was whether dNRXN3 heterozygosity would protect against mHTT pathogenesis in neurons. Interestingly, the answer was no (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Glia-specific knockdown of dNRXN3 mitigated mHTT toxicity in glia.
source: Consistent with this, glia-specific knockdown of dNRXN3 (using the repo-GAL4 driver) mitigated mHTT toxicity in glia (Figure 4B, left panel), but neuron-specific knockdown (using the elav-GAL4 driver) of dNRXN3 did not mitigate mHTT toxicity in neurons (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Neuron-specific knockdown of dNRXN3 did not mitigate mHTT toxicity in neurons.
source: Consistent with this, glia-specific knockdown of dNRXN3 (using the repo-GAL4 driver) mitigated mHTT toxicity in glia (Figure 4B, left panel), but neuron-specific knockdown (using the elav-GAL4 driver) of dNRXN3 did not mitigate mHTT toxicity in neurons (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Reducing dNRXN3 in both neurons and glia protects against glial pathogenesis and the combination of neuronal and glial pathogenesis, but not neuronal pathogenesis.
source: In sum, reducing dNRXN3 in both neurons and glia protects against glial pathogenesis—and the combination of neuronal and glial pathogenesis—but not neuronal pathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral assay results showing differential effects of dNRXN3 reduction in different cell types.

claim: Lowering expression of dNRXN3 in glia is necessary and sufficient to mitigate behavioral impairments caused by mHTT.
source: This implies that mHTT disrupts some aspect of glial-neuronal interaction that is driven by the glia since lowering expression of dNRXN3 in glia is necessary and sufficient to mitigate behavioral impairments caused by mHTT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral assay results showing that glial-specific dNRXN3 knockdown is protective.

claim: Nrxn3 is expressed in striatal astrocytes in HD mice.
source: To investigate whether Nrxn3 is expressed in astrocytes in the striatum of HD mice, we performed in situ hybridization (ISH) in coronal sections of striatal tissue taken from a mouse model of HD (HdhzQ175/+) to probe Nrxn3 mRNA. Nrxn3 was expressed in striatal astrocytes (Figure 4C, D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 4C, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 25 genes with altered expression in HD suppressed mHTT-induced behavioral deficits in neurons, glia, or both.
source: In all, we identified 25 genes with altered expression in HD that suppressed mHTT-induced behavioral deficits in neurons, glia, or both (Figure 5B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on high-throughput behavioral screening of 411 alleles representing 248 Drosophila genes.

claim: Many of the modifiers common to neuronal and glial mHTT-induced dysfunction are involved in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (RHOC, TIAM1, ENAH, and CFL2), vesicular trafficking (SNAP23, SNX9, and SNX18), and inflammation (JUN, GTF3A, and ATF3).
source: Many of the modifiers common to neuronal and glial mHTT-induced dysfunction are involved in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton (RHOC, TIAM1, ENAH, and CFL2), vesicular trafficking (SNAP23, SNX9, and SNX18), and inflammation (JUN, GTF3A, and ATF3).
evidence: The claim is based on functional annotation of genes identified in the behavioral screen.

claim: Knockdown of Spn42De (dSERPINA1) in Drosophila expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia mitigated behavioral impairments.
source: Knockdown of Spn42De (henceforth dSERPINA1) in Drosophila expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia mitigated behavioral impairments (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: dSERPINA1 knockdown consistently reduced mHTT protein levels in lysates extracted from the heads of Drosophila expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia.
source: In independent immunoblots, dSERPINA1 knockdown consistently reduced mHTT protein levels in lysates extracted from the heads of Drosophila expressing mHTT in both neurons and glia (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: The claim is based on western blot data presented in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Serpina1a knockdown significantly reduced mHTT signal in HdhQ111/Q7 mouse striatal cell lysates.
source: To validate this observation across model systems, we performed homogenous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) on HdhQ111/Q7 mouse striatal cell lysates that were treated with either a pool of non-targeting scramble small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), a pool of siRNAs against Htt, or a pool of siRNAs against Serpina1a (the murine ortholog of SERPINA1). Serpina1a knockdown significantly reduced mHTT signal (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on HTRF data from mouse striatal cells presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Knockdown of SERPINA1 protected against mHTT toxicity in neurons and glia by reducing levels of mutant HTT.
source: Knockdown of SERPINA1 thus protected against mHTT toxicity in neurons and glia by reducing levels of mutant HTT.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral and protein level data showing that SERPINA1 knockdown both improves behavior and reduces mHTT levels.

claim: Serpina1a protein staining was increased in the striatum of HdhzQ175/+ compared to wildtype mice at 8.5 months.
source: We found increased Serpina1a protein staining in the striatum of HdhzQ175/+ compared to wildtype mice at 8.5 months (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), confirming its upregulation from the transcriptomic data.
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a high degree of overlap of DEGs across tissues from human HD brains, brains of HD mice, and flies that express mHTT in glia.
source: We found a high degree of overlap of DEGs across tissues from human HD brains, brains of HD mice, and flies that express mHTT in glia.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparative transcriptomic analysis showing concordant DEGs across species.

claim: Drosophila glia perform many of the same functions as mammalian astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and microglia including phagocytosis.
source: Our observations are however consistent with previous evidence that Drosophila glia perform many of the same functions as mammalian astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and microglia including phagocytosis (Chung et al., 2020; Freeman, 2015; Freeman and Doherty, 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Chung et al., 2020; Freeman, 2015; Freeman and Doherty, 2006; Ziegenfuss et al., 2012).

claim: Wildtype glial cells ameliorate disease when transplanted into HD mice.
source: Several studies have also shown that wildtype glial cells ameliorate disease when transplanted into HD mice, and mHTT exerts a deleterious effect on glial development and function, which in turn influences HD pathogenesis (Benraiss et al., 2016; Bradford et al., 2009; Garcia et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015; Osipovitch et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Benraiss et al., 2016; Bradford et al., 2009; Garcia et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015; Osipovitch et al., 2019).

claim: Transcription factors involved in glial differentiation and myelin synthesis are downregulated in glial progenitor cells in HD.
source: More recently, it was discovered that transcription factors involved in glial differentiation and myelin synthesis are downregulated in glial progenitor cells (Osipovitch et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Osipovitch et al., 2019.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction is a common theme among many neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Synaptic dysfunction is a common theme among many neurodegenerative disorders (McInnes et al., 2018; Phan et al., 2017; Prots et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (McInnes et al., 2018; Phan et al., 2017; Prots et al., 2018).

claim: The expression of mHTT in glia is sufficient to drive synaptic dysfunction.
source: Our results support the observation that the expression of mHTT in glia is sufficient to drive synaptic dysfunction (Wood et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wood et al., 2018, and is consistent with the findings of this study.

claim: In HD, pre-synaptic neurons release elevated levels of glutamate into the synapse, driving medium spiny neurons (MSNs) into excitotoxicity.
source: In HD, pre-synaptic neurons release elevated levels of glutamate into the synapse, driving medium spiny neurons (MSNs) into excitotoxicity (Estrada Sánchez et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Estrada Sánchez et al., 2008 and Hong et al., 2016.

claim: Hyperactivity of receptors at the post-synaptic densities sensitizes MSNs to excitotoxicity, further contributing to neurodegeneration.
source: Hyperactivity of receptors at the post-synaptic densities sensitizes MSNs to excitotoxicity, further contributing to neurodegeneration (Estrada Sánchez et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Estrada Sánchez et al., 2008.

claim: Astrocytic mHTT expression may contribute to neuronal excitotoxicity by elevating levels of glutamate, potassium, and calcium at the synapse.
source: Astrocytic mHTT expression may contribute to neuronal excitotoxicity by elevating levels of glutamate, potassium, and calcium at the synapse (Garcia et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garcia et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; and Tong et al., 2014.

claim: Metabotropic glutamate receptors and the scaffold protein HOMER1 regulate calcium and glutamate signaling in astrocytes.
source: Modifiers of mHTT-induced pathogenesis identified in our study, such as metabotropic glutamate receptors and the scaffold protein HOMER1, regulate calcium and glutamate signaling in astrocytes (Buscemi et al., 2017; Spampinato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buscemi et al., 2017 and Spampinato et al., 2018.

claim: Glial calcium signaling can influence neuronal activity at the neuronal soma.
source: Glial calcium signaling can also influence neuronal activity, however, at the neuronal soma (Weiss et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2019.

claim: In Drosophila, cortical glia modulate neuronal activity through potassium buffering, a process that is regulated by calcium-mediated endocytosis of potassium channels.
source: In Drosophila, cortical glia modulate neuronal activity through potassium buffering, a process that is regulated by calcium-mediated endocytosis of potassium channels (Weiss et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2019.

claim: In HD, the distances between astrocytes and pre-synaptic neurons are increased at the cortico-striatal circuit.
source: Glia can also physically disrupt synapses in disease states: Förster resonance energy transmission in vivo revealed that, in HD, the distances between astrocytes and pre-synaptic neurons are increased at the cortico-striatal circuit (Octeau et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Octeau et al., 2018.

claim: Downregulating synaptic function is protective in HD because it attenuates the excitotoxicity that characterizes the disease.
source: This supports a model in which dampening synaptic function is protective because it attenuates the excitotoxicity that characterizes HD.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed by the authors based on their findings and previous knowledge about HD excitotoxicity.

claim: Mutant HTT disrupts neuronal development.
source: Mutant HTT disrupts neuronal development (Ring et al., 2015) and skews embryonic neurogenesis toward producing more neurons (Barnat et al., 2020); by the time HD mutation carriers reach the age of 6 years, they have greatly enlarged striata and functional hyperconnectivity to the cerebellum (Tereshchenko et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ring et al., 2015; Barnat et al., 2020; and Tereshchenko et al., 2020.

claim: Mutant HTT skews embryonic neurogenesis toward producing more neurons.
source: Mutant HTT disrupts neuronal development (Ring et al., 2015) and skews embryonic neurogenesis toward producing more neurons (Barnat et al., 2020); by the time HD mutation carriers reach the age of 6 years, they have greatly enlarged striata and functional hyperconnectivity to the cerebellum (Tereshchenko et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnat et al., 2020.

claim: By the time HD mutation carriers reach the age of 6 years, they have greatly enlarged striata and functional hyperconnectivity to the cerebellum.
source: Mutant HTT disrupts neuronal development (Ring et al., 2015) and skews embryonic neurogenesis toward producing more neurons (Barnat et al., 2020); by the time HD mutation carriers reach the age of 6 years, they have greatly enlarged striata and functional hyperconnectivity to the cerebellum (Tereshchenko et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tereshchenko et al., 2020.

claim: The more hyperconnected the brain, the more abrupt the loss of these connections, and the more rapid the striatal atrophy that follows.
source: The more hyperconnected, the more abrupt the loss of these connections, and the more rapid the striatal atrophy that follows Tereshchenko et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tereshchenko et al., 2020.

claim: Deletion of astrocytic neurexin-1α attenuates synaptic transmission but not synapse number.
source: The recent observation that deletion of astrocytic neurexin-1α attenuates synaptic transmission but not synapse number supports this hypothesis (Trotter et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trotter et al., 2020.

claim: In astrocytes, calcium signaling controls the activity of reactive astrocytes.
source: In astrocytes, calcium signaling also controls the activity of reactive astrocytes (Buscemi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buscemi et al., 2017.

claim: Astrogliosis is typically observed at later stages of HD.
source: Astrogliosis, or the proliferation of immune active astrocytes, is typically observed at later stages of HD (Al-Dalahmah et al., 2020; Buscemi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Al-Dalahmah et al., 2020 and Buscemi et al., 2017.

claim: Immune-activated glia eliminate synapses.
source: These immune-activated glia not only eliminate synapses (Liddelow et al., 2017; Sofroniew, 2009) but can also transmit mHTT aggregates through the synapse (Donnelly et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liddelow et al., 2017 and Sofroniew, 2009.

claim: Immune-activated glia can transmit mHTT aggregates through the synapse.
source: These immune-activated glia not only eliminate synapses (Liddelow et al., 2017; Sofroniew, 2009) but can also transmit mHTT aggregates through the synapse (Donnelly et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Donnelly et al., 2020.

claim: In Drosophila, knockdown of draper prevents astrocytic phagocytosis and stops the spread of mHTT protein aggregates from pre-synaptic neurons to the post-synaptic compartment.
source: In Drosophila, knockdown of draper prevents astrocytic phagocytosis and stops the spread of mHTT protein aggregates from pre-synaptic neurons to the post-synaptic compartment (Donnelly et al., 2020; Pearce et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Donnelly et al., 2020 and Pearce et al., 2015.

claim: mHTT protein can enter the synaptic space by endosomal/lysosomal secretion mediated by Syt7.
source: mHTT protein can also enter the synaptic space by endosomal/lysosomal secretion mediated by Syt7 (Trajkovic et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Trajkovic et al., 2017.

claim: Loss-of-function variants in NRXN1-3, NLGN1, NLGN3, DLGAP3, and LRRTM1 have been associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).
source: Intriguingly, loss-of-function variants in NRXN1-3, NLGN1, NLGN3, DLGAP3, and LRRTM1 have been associated with various disorders of synaptic dysfunction, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) (Nakanishi et al., 2017; Jamain et al., 2003; Südhof, 2008; Vaags et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Windrem et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Nakanishi et al., 2017; Jamain et al., 2003; Südhof, 2008; Vaags et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Windrem et al., 2017).

claim: Many HD patients develop schizophrenia-like psychosis.
source: It is interesting that many HD patients develop schizophrenia-like psychosis, suggesting that the compensatory mechanism at place in HD may eventually lead to schizophrenia-like symptoms (Connors et al., 2020; Tsuang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Connors et al., 2020 and Tsuang et al., 2018.

claim: The greatest differences between RNA-seq samples are attributable to the cell-specific drivers, and not to the use of N-terminal versus full-length protein.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the greatest differences between samples are attributable to the cell-specific drivers, and not to the use of N-terminal versus full-length protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on PCA analysis of RNA-seq samples presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Modulating the expression of genes other than mHTT in glia could be an effective strategy for ameliorating HD-induced CNS dysfunction.
source: In conclusion, modulating the expression genes other than mHTT in glia could be an effective strategy for ameliorating HD-induced central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the findings that reducing expression of various glial genes improves HD phenotypes.

claim: SERPINA1 expression is low in the healthy brain but it is upregulated in several disease conditions.
source: Interestingly, SERPINA1 expression is low in the healthy brain but it is upregulated in several disease conditions, consistent with a potential role in neuroinflammation (Abu-Rumeileh et al., 2020; Cabezas-Llobet et al., 2018; Gollin et al., 1992; Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research (Abu-Rumeileh et al., 2020; Cabezas-Llobet et al., 2018; Gollin et al., 1992; Peng et al., 2015).

claim: Downregulation of glial genes involved in synaptic function mitigates Huntington's disease pathogenesis.
source: A large portion of conserved genes are concordantly dysregulated across the three species; we tested these genes in a high-throughput behavioral assay and found that downregulation of genes involved in synapse assembly mitigated pathogenesis and behavioral deficits.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study, supported by transcriptomic analysis and behavioral assays.

claim: Reducing dNRXN3 function in glia was sufficient to improve the phenotype of flies expressing mHTT in neurons.
source: To our surprise, reducing dNRXN3 function in glia was sufficient to improve the phenotype of flies expressing mHTT in neurons, suggesting that mHTT's toxic effects in glia ramify throughout the brain.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral assay data showing that glial-specific dNRXN3 knockdown improves neuronal mHTT phenotypes.

claim: Dampening synaptic function is protective in HD because it attenuates the excitotoxicity that characterizes the disease.
source: This supports a model in which dampening synaptic function is protective because it attenuates the excitotoxicity that characterizes HD.
evidence: The claim is a model proposed by the authors based on their findings and previous knowledge about HD excitotoxicity.
